name: Depression and Mood
title: When getting through the day takes more than people can see.
summary: Depression can affect interest, energy, relationships, and the way you see yourself. Understand the patterns, the role of assessment, and what a practical treatment conversation can involve.
cardSummary: Low mood is not the only experience worth noticing. Explore lost interest, withdrawal, self-criticism, and changes in everyday functioning, with a worked example of how a smaller next step differs from being told to try harder.

panel.title: You do not have to look unwell to need support.
paragraphs: You might still be working, parenting, or replying to messages while feeling disconnected from the life you are maintaining. Start with that difference between what others see and what it costs you.

items.title: Understand the concern
items.text: Mood, interest, energy, and daily life.

items.title: See an everyday example
items.text: The invitation that keeps getting postponed.

sections.title: Look at the pattern, not a single feeling.
paragraphs: Depression is different from an occasional low day. Persistent low mood or loss of interest can appear alongside changes in sleep, appetite, concentration, energy, and feelings of worth. Not everyone has every symptom. The combination, duration, distress, and effect on daily life matter more than recognizing yourself in one sentence.

An assessment considers what has changed, how long it has been happening, and what else might contribute. Health conditions, medication effects, substance use, sleep, and periods of unusually elevated or irritable mood can affect the picture. A page about depression cannot make those distinctions for you.

A useful first description does not have to sound clinical: I am doing what is expected, but nothing feels rewarding; I keep putting off things that used to matter; or I am much more irritable than I recognize. Those are starting points for understanding, not evidence that you have failed.

panel.title: Functioning and feeling well are not the same question.
paragraphs: Instead of using productivity as the only measure, consider what feels absent, what takes extra effort, and what you have stopped doing. Bring your own examples rather than trying to match a stereotype.

sections.title: What has become harder, smaller, or less meaningful?
sections.intro: These are illustrative descriptions to help you find words, not a screening checklist.

items.title: The day is full. You feel empty.
items.teaser: Tasks are completed without much connection to them.
paragraphs: Imagine finishing a demanding week and finding no satisfaction in anything you accomplished. A helpful description might separate the outside routine from the inside experience: what you still do, what you no longer enjoy, and how much recovery each day seems to require.
You do not need to prove that things have become visibly chaotic before explaining that they feel different.

items.title: Everything is waiting for more energy.
items.teaser: Messages, meals, and decisions keep moving to tomorrow.
paragraphs: An ordinary task can have several parts: starting, deciding, organizing, and tolerating the feelings it brings up. In an appointment, describing where you get stuck can be more informative than calling yourself unmotivated.
A plan should consider your actual capacity and health, rather than simply add more obligations to a list that already feels impossible.

items.title: You have become your own harshest critic.
items.teaser: A missed task becomes a conclusion about your whole character.
paragraphs: Compare an event with the judgment attached to it. I did not return that call describes something that happened. I am a burden tells a much larger story. Both can be discussed without insisting that you replace them with cheerful statements you do not believe.
The aim of this example is clearer language for a conversation, not an instruction to argue yourself out of distress.

sections.title: The invitation you keep meaning to answer.
sections.intro: A small fictional moment can show why motivation is not the whole story.

items.title: What happens
paragraphs: Morgan receives an invitation from a friend. Meeting up once felt easy; now choosing a time, getting ready, and making conversation seem exhausting.

items.title: What follows
paragraphs: Morgan postpones replying, then feels embarrassed about the delay. The next message becomes harder to answer, and the weekend feels increasingly isolated.

items.title: What could be explored
paragraphs: A therapist might help Morgan understand the fatigue, self-judgment, and withdrawal separately. They could discuss a more manageable kind of contact while assessing the wider mood and health picture.

reveal.title: Why not simply say yes and push through?
paragraphs: The useful question is not whether Morgan can perform a bigger task. It is what is contributing to the difficulty and what kind of change would be realistic. A short call, a different time, or an honest reply might be possibilities to discuss, not assignments that apply to everyone.

Progress would include how the experience actually felt and whether functioning, connection, or mood changed over time. A difficult week would be information for revising the plan, not proof that Morgan did not want to improve.

sections.title: Understanding first. A plan you can participate in.
sections.intro: This is a planning framework, not a prescribed session sequence.

items.title: Describe the whole picture
paragraphs: Discuss changes in mood, interest, sleep, relationships, health, and safety. Share what helps temporarily and what has stopped helping. A clinician can explain which questions need further assessment.

items.title: Choose a meaningful target
paragraphs: A first goal might concern getting through mornings, reconnecting with someone, or reducing the impact of self-criticism. The target should be recognizable in your life, not only on a questionnaire.

items.title: Connect a method to the target
paragraphs: CBT can address unhelpful thinking and behavior patterns. Other treatment options may be appropriate, including care coordinated with a prescribing or medical professional. Ask how the suggested work relates to your particular needs.

items.title: Review and adjust
paragraphs: Discuss whether the work feels usable and whether your symptoms and daily functioning are changing. An unchanged or worsening picture calls for review, not indefinite repetition of the same plan.

sections.title: Support is not a demand for positivity.

items.title: Encouragement versus explanation
paragraphs: Reassurance may be kind without answering why life has become harder. You can ask for help understanding the pattern as well as support getting through it.

items.title: Ordinary booking versus urgent help
paragraphs: Do not wait for a routine consultation if you may harm yourself or cannot stay safe. In the U.S., call or text 988 for crisis support. Call 911 for immediate life-threatening danger.

sections.title: You can ask for help before you have the answers.

items.question: Do I need a depression diagnosis before contacting you?
paragraphs: No. Describe what has been difficult and ask about an appropriate clinical starting appointment. A brief introductory consultation is different from the fuller assessment needed to understand symptoms and plan care.

items.question: Does therapy mean I must take medication?
paragraphs: No. Psychotherapy and medication are different options that may be used separately or together. The choice should reflect your needs and medical situation. Do not start or stop medication based on this guide; discuss it with a qualified prescriber.

items.question: What if sadness is not the main thing I feel?
paragraphs: Loss of interest, irritability, low energy, or difficulty concentrating can also be relevant. They do not establish depression on their own. Describe the change rather than trying to fit yourself into a single picture.

items.question: What can I bring to a first appointment?
paragraphs: An optional private note can describe a typical day, what feels different, and one thing you hope would become easier. Keep detailed health information for the clinician's approved intake process rather than a public website or email inquiry.
